title: Constructors and properties
summary: Make sure every object starts out valid, and control how its data is read and changed.

steps.title: Constructors: born ready
body: With plain fields, a new object starts empty and you hope someone fills it in. Forget one line and you have a customer with no name.
A **constructor** closes that gap. It is a special method that runs during `new`, and it can demand the data the object needs.
```csharp
Customer c = new Customer("Maya");
Console.WriteLine(c.Name);   // Maya
class Customer
public string Name;
public Customer(string name)
Name = name;
- A constructor has the **same name as the class** and **no return type**.
- Once you write one that takes parameters, `new Customer()` with no arguments stops compiling. That is the point: a customer without a name can no longer exist.
> **Tip:** This is also why the last lesson needed `= ""` on string fields. The compiler warns when a `string` could be left empty. A constructor that always sets it removes the warning properly.

steps.prompt: What happens on the first line?
options: It does not compile: the only constructor needs a `sku` and a `quantity`
It creates a line with `Sku` empty and `Quantity` 0
It compiles, then crashes when the program runs
It creates a line and asks the user for the values
steps.explain: A class only gets a free no-argument constructor when you write none yourself. Here the compiler forces every caller to supply both values.

steps.title: Properties
body: Public fields let anyone change anything at any time. C# code almost always uses **properties** instead. A property looks like a field from outside, but you decide who may read it and who may write it.
```csharp
class OrderLine
public string Sku { get; }             // read-only after construction
public int Quantity { get; set; }      // read and write
public decimal UnitPrice { get; }
public decimal Total => UnitPrice * Quantity;   // computed on every read
public OrderLine(string sku, decimal unitPrice, int quantity)
Sku = sku;
UnitPrice = unitPrice;
Quantity = quantity;
- `{ get; set; }` is an **auto-property**: C# stores the value for you.
- `{ get; }` has no setter. Only the constructor can assign it.
- `=> expression` stores nothing. `Total` is worked out fresh each time, so it can never be out of date.
You use them exactly like fields: `line.Quantity = 3;` and `line.Total`.

steps.prompt: A customer's name is fixed at creation. Their email can be changed later.
steps.explain: `{ get; }` can only be assigned in the constructor. `{ get; set; }` can be assigned by anyone, any time.

steps.prompt: `Total` is a computed property. What does this print?
code: public OrderLine(string sku, decimal unitPrice, int quantity)
steps.explain: `Total` is recalculated on every read, so it follows `Quantity` automatically. Nobody has to remember to update it.

steps.title: An estimate that formats itself
prompt: Write a class `Estimate` for how long a task should take. Your `Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes)` from First steps is ready to call.
- a read-only property `int Minutes` set by the constructor;
- a computed property `string Text` that returns `Sk.FormatMinutes(Minutes)`;
- a computed property `bool IsLong` that is `true` above 120 minutes.
template: Dojo.Eq("90 minutes is not long", false, dojoE.IsLong);
Dojo.Eq("150 minutes is long", true, new Estimate(150).IsLong);
Dojo.Eq("120 minutes is not long", false, new Estimate(120).IsLong);
Dojo.Check("Minutes cannot be set from outside", typeof(Estimate).GetProperty("Minutes")?.SetMethod is null, "use { get; } so only the constructor sets it");
hints: `public int Minutes { get; }` can only be set in the constructor.
`public string Text => Sk.FormatMinutes(Minutes);` is computed every time it is read.

steps.title: Object initialisers, init and required
body: Constructors with six parameters are hard to read: which `""` was the postcode? An **object initialiser** names each value instead.
```csharp
var label = new ShippingLabel
Recipient = "Maya Okafor",
City = "Leeds"
class ShippingLabel
public required string Recipient { get; init; }
public required string City { get; init; }
public string Country { get; init; } = "UK";
- `init` is a setter that only works **while the object is being created**. Afterwards the property is read-only.
- `required` makes the compiler reject any `new ShippingLabel { ... }` that leaves the property out.
- `= "UK"` is a default. Callers may override it or skip it.
Together they give you the safety of a constructor with the readability of names.

steps.prompt: Given this `ShippingLabel` class, what happens here?
code: var label = new ShippingLabel { Recipient = "Maya", City = "Leeds" };
public required string Recipient { get; init; }
public required string City { get; init; }
options: Line 2 does not compile: an `init` property can only be set during creation
Line 1 does not compile: `Country` was not set
It runs and the city becomes York
It compiles, then throws an exception on line 2
steps.explain: `Country` has a default, so leaving it out is fine. `City` is `init`-only, and the compiler enforces that. No running program can ever change it.

steps.title: Validate in the constructor
body: A constructor can do more than copy values. It can **refuse** bad ones.
```csharp fragment
public OrderLine(string sku, int quantity)
if (quantity <= 0)
throw new ArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
Sku = sku;
Quantity = quantity;

`throw` stops the constructor on the spot. No object is created, and the caller gets an error instead of a broken order line. (Exceptions get a full lesson in the next module. For now: `throw new ArgumentException("message")` means *you gave me a bad argument*.)
This is the real payoff. If the only way to make an `OrderLine` is through a constructor that checks, then **every `OrderLine` in your program is valid**. No other code has to check again.

steps.prompt: Build the constructor: check the quantity first, then store `Sku`, then `Quantity`.
lines: throw new ArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
steps.explain: Checks go first, so a bad value is rejected before anything is stored.

steps.title: Sidekick piece: TaskItem, valid from the start
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** Your `TaskItem` from the last lesson can be built broken: no title, negative minutes, a timer stopped before it started. Rebuild it so **every task is valid from the start**. Sidekick's `sk add` makes tasks only through this constructor.
- `id` below 1: `throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.")`;
- empty or blank `title`: `throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title))`;
- negative estimate: `throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.")`;
Properties, all readable, none settable from outside: `Id`, `Title`, `EstimateMinutes` (get-only) and `LoggedMinutes`, `IsRunning`, `StartedAt` (a `DateTime`), `Done` (`{ get; private set; }`).
- `Start(DateTime at)`: a `Done` task throws `InvalidOperationException`; already running does nothing; otherwise sets `StartedAt` and `IsRunning`.
- `int Stop(DateTime at)`: not running returns 0; `at` before `StartedAt` throws `ArgumentException` (the timer keeps running); otherwise adds and returns the whole minutes, like before.
- `Log(int minutes)`: adds minutes logged by hand; below 1 throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `Complete()`: sets `Done` and stops the timer (`IsRunning = false`, without logging).
`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)` tells you whether a title is blank.
starter: public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
solution: public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
template: var dojoT = new TaskItem(1, "  Fix login  ", 45);
Dojo.Eq("the title is trimmed", "Fix login", dojoT.Title);
Dojo.Eq("the estimate defaults to 0", 0, new TaskItem(2, "Docs").EstimateMinutes);
Dojo.Eq("a new task is not done", false, dojoT.Done);
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("a blank title is refused", () => new TaskItem(3, "   "));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("a negative estimate is refused", () => new TaskItem(4, "x", -5));
Dojo.Eq("StartedAt is remembered", new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0), dojoT.StartedAt);
Dojo.Eq("Stop returns the minutes", 50, dojoT.Stop(new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 50, 0)));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("stopping before the start is refused", () => dojoT.Stop(new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("after a refused Stop the timer still runs", true, dojoT.IsRunning);
Dojo.Eq("then a real Stop works", 10, dojoT.Stop(new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 10, 10, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("Complete stops the timer", false, dojoT.IsRunning);
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("a done task cannot start", () => dojoT.Start(new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 12, 0, 0)));
Dojo.Check("Title cannot be changed from outside", typeof(TaskItem).GetProperty("Title")?.SetMethod is null, "make Title get-only");
Dojo.Check("LoggedMinutes has no public setter", typeof(TaskItem).GetProperty("LoggedMinutes")?.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "use { get; private set; }");
Dojo.Check("Done has no public setter", typeof(TaskItem).GetProperty("Done")?.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "use { get; private set; }");
hints: The constructor checks first, each with its own `if (...) throw ...;`, and only then stores `Id`, `Title = title.Trim()` and `EstimateMinutes`.
`Stop`: after `if (!IsRunning) return 0;` add `if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));`.
`Log` checks `minutes < 1` then adds; `Complete` sets `IsRunning = false; Done = true;`.
steps.explain: Every rule now lives in one place. Anyone holding a `TaskItem` knows it has a title, a sensible estimate and a timer that never ran backwards, without checking again.
